November margins are at -$22.65 cpg ex-Ulsan and -$25.35 cpg ex-Singapore, against roughly +$20 cpg on 9 September, a swing of about 43 cpg in under a week. October is no better at -$20.85 cpg from Ulsan, and December only recovers to -$11.25 cpg from Ulsan and -$14.95 cpg from Singapore. These arbs are almost always open, which makes this a structural bearish change for MR demand. There have been no fixtures to West Coast Americas since 9 September. Bearish for regional MR tonnage demand, but demand into Oceania remains robust.

For context, if we get half capacity East-West pipeline "within days" and then a full return in 6 weeks, that still means Saudi Arabia has lost ~3.5 MMbpd of export capacity out its Red Sea coast for the next month and a half.

Riyadh's recent Gulf export drive gonna continue.

text:
*SAUDIS SEEK TO RESUME HALF OF KEY OIL PIPELINE WITHIN DAYS

Crude swoons. https://t.co/Q6zajuQ6Sy

If the Saudis manage to resume partial flow it confirms that the damage was isolated to pumping stations and there wasn't any serious damage to the pipeline itself.

You can run a pipeline with fewer pumping stations at lower pressure (thus capacity).

Should note that even if the pipeline is resumed at half capacity, we'd still see more than a 50% decline from pre-attack Saudi Red Sea exports.

Saudi west coast has 1-1.5 MMbpd of domestic refiner demand, which will be prioritized.

So very rough full capacity EW = 7 MMbpd, 1.5 goes to refineries and 5.5 MMbpd is exported.

Pipe comes back at 50% (3.5 MMbpd), 1.5 would go to domestic use and 2 would be exported.

Will work today to fine tune those numbers further.

Bolivia's government announced Sept. 15 it will triple a fund to finance refined fuel purchases, following similar moves by fellow Andean countries Peru and Ecuador to mitigate diesel shortages and rising prices.

Supreme Decree 5705 increased a Bolivian government fund to 6 billion bolivianos ($500 million) from 2 billion bolivianos "to maintain stabilization measures for petroleum derivatives and guarantee nationwide fuel supply," according to the state gazette.

The government of President Rodrigo Paz, which is struggling to turn around Bolivia's crippled economy after 20 years of statist policies, is battling chronic diesel shortages amidst sporadic protests by transport workers over fuel price increases. The government earlier this month decreed state oil company YPFB will pull out of refined fuel distribution, allowing private operators to take charge of the country's downstream sector. YPFB is also cracking down on fuel contraband, which it blames for diesel shortages.

Neighboring countries Peru and Ecuador, meanwhile, have increased fuel subsidies and efforts to ramp up production at state oil refineries.

Gold is heading into the FOMC meeting up 1.5% at USD 4,355 on the day, suggesting a rate hike is all but priced in. What happens next will likely depend on Warsh and, importantly, how the hike is “sold” to the market.

The relatively steep downtrend from the August high from around USD 4,700 is currently being tested, potentially shifting attention to a USD 4,420-40 band of resistance. A break above these levels would strengthen the case for a more sustained recovery, back towards the 200-day moving average at USD 4,540, while failure would point to more consolidation.

Brent near USD 110 is masking a much tighter physical oil market. Saudi pipeline disruptions have pushed Dated Brent above USD 130, while diesel has surged beyond USD 220 as refiners scramble for scarce barrels and export curbs loom. https://t.co/0rTtjBVVzV via @saxobank

#Commodities
Brent #crude settled near USD 109 on Tuesday, extending its September gain to almost 20%, after talks on a temporary Hormuz shipping corridor were reportedly postponed. Prices have eased this morning as some risk premium unwinds after the API reported a weekly rise in US crude and fuel stockpiles, while data showed flows through the Strait of Hormuz rising to their highest since June/July. However, the pickup is only partly offsetting lost export barrels following drone attacks that shut Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, for which there is still no restart timeline. The resulting squeeze on prompt supply and Saudi Aramco delaying deliveries to European customers has pushed Dated Brent above USD 130 per barrel as physical-market traders price an increased risk of near-term supply shortages.

#Gold has moved back above USD 4,300, finding renewed demand below that level as traders conclude that a US rate hike today is largely priced in, while some profit-taking on short bond positions has also supported the rebound. Recent pressure has reflected a combination of rising oil prices, a now fully priced US rate hike, a stronger dollar and, not least, long-end bond yields reaching levels last seen in 2023. The coming days will show whether demand from less interest-rate-sensitive investors seeking protection against fiscal and geopolitical risks is sufficient to prevent a deeper correction. In our view, a move back above USD 4,350 and not least USD 4,425 is needed to ease the current downside pressure.
